content: Studies that evaluated policies using government-led nutrient profile models were more likely to report favorable effects on reducing exposure to unhealthy food marketing compared to those using company-led models. For instance, only six out of six studies on government-led models reported positive outcomes, whereas eight out of 25 studies on company-led models showed similar results. Furthermore, studies on company-led models were more likely to report unfavorable effects on exposure, unlike those on government-led models. Some studies also examined the migration of marketing efforts following policy implementation. For example, after the UK banned television advertising of high-fat, sugar, and salt (HFSS) foods on children’s channels and during programs appealing to children, there was no significant change in children’s exposure to HFSS advertising. This was attributed to a shift in advertising to other times and channels that children also watched. Similarly, in the US, a policy targeting children under 12 led to a decrease in food and beverage advertisements viewed by 2–11-year-olds but an increase for 12–17-year-olds, indicating a migration of marketing to non-restricted spaces. Eighteen studies assessed the impact of food marketing policies on the power of food marketing. Among these, three studies reported clear positive effects favoring the intervention, two showed unclear but potentially positive effects, one found no effect, six reported unclear effects potentially favoring the control, and six reported clear effects favoring the control. Studies comparing mandatory policies with no policy were more likely to report positive effects favoring the intervention (100% of studies) than those comparing voluntary policies with no policy (8% of studies). Voluntary policies were more likely to show unfavorable effects on public health compared to mandatory policies. Policies restricting food marketing to children, including those older than 12 years, were more likely to report favorable effects on reducing marketing power than policies targeting only children aged 12 or younger. For example, three out of four studies on broader age policies reported positive effects, compared to one out of 12 studies on policies targeting younger children. Policies targeting only younger children were more likely to report unfavorable effects, unlike those targeting a broader age range. Studies evaluating policies restricting promotional characters were more likely to report favorable effects (three out of 10 studies) compared to those restricting a broader range of child-appealing techniques (one out of five studies) or animation techniques (zero out of one study). Most of these studies assessed voluntary policies. Policies addressing television food marketing or packaging were more likely to report favorable effects than those addressing digital marketing, where no studies reported positive outcomes. Five studies examined the impact of food marketing policies on food purchasing. Four reported clear positive effects favoring the intervention, while one reported effects favoring the control. One study assessed dietary intake and reported clear positive effects favoring the intervention. Two studies evaluated product changes, with one reporting no effect and the other favoring the control. Three studies examined unintended societal consequences, with one showing a significant reduction in HFSS advertising expenditure and two reporting unclear but potentially positive effects. A total of 244 publications reviewed contextual factors influencing the implementation of food marketing policies. In high-income countries (HICs), overweight and obesity were generally perceived as serious health issues, especially among women and individuals of lower socioeconomic status (SES). In contrast, in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), overweight and obesity were often seen as indicators of good health, though this perception is changing in some regions. There was no variability in the negative perception of diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and dental issues across studies. Evidence on resource implications showed that policies to protect children from harmful food marketing are cost-effective or cost-saving. Costs included planning, implementation, and compliance, while savings typically involved healthcare cost reductions. Self-regulation was found to be less costly but also less effective due to presumed lower compliance. Strong political leadership, supporting evidence, intersectoral collaboration, and community support facilitated policy development and implementation, while barriers included regulatory complexity, conflicting interests, and resource limitations. Fifty-nine publications highlighted the alignment of such policies with human rights standards, including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. These frameworks emphasize children’s rights to health, adequate nutrition, and protection from exploitation. Unregulated food marketing was noted to undermine these rights. The Committee on the Rights of the Child has called for regulation of HFSS food marketing, particularly in digital environments, to protect children’s best interests. Limited evidence was found on the impact of these policies on health equity. However, research from HICs indicates that children from lower SES backgrounds are more exposed to food marketing, exacerbating health inequities. Policies restricting food marketing can reduce these disparities, as shown in a modeling study from Australia, which found greater health benefits and cost savings for lower SES children. Evidence on acceptability varied by stakeholder. Policies were generally acceptable to governments and policymakers, as indicated by their inclusion in national action plans. Public support was higher among women and varied by age, ethnicity, and SES. Industry opposition to government-led restrictions was common, with voluntary self-regulation often proposed as an alternative. However, such self-regulation was seen as a strategy to prevent stronger government regulations. Feasibility evidence showed that existing policies in some countries demonstrate their practicality, though many nations have yet to implement such measures. Facilitators included clear guidelines, independent monitoring, and transparency, while barriers included lack of resources, industry interference, and methodological challenges. In summary, children of all ages should be protected from marketing of foods high in saturated fats, trans fats, free sugars, and salt. This aligns with human rights standards and public health goals, emphasizing the need for comprehensive, enforceable policies to safeguard children’s health and well-being.
